screens.title: ROS Command-Line Tools and Logging
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn to use ROS’s command-line toolkit and logging system so you can inspect running nodes, monitor topic traffic, call services, manage parameters, and find the log files that explain failures. These commands are your primary debugging tools — they let you explore the system without editing code and they help you isolate where messages, services, or configuration are going wrong. We’ll show concrete terminal examples so you can practice listing nodes, echoing topic messages, calling services, and changing logging levels. You will also learn where ROS stores log files and how the logging severity levels map to practical debugging choices. By the end you should be able to follow a simple diagnostic checklist when a node stops responding and find the log entry or service error that explains the failure. Keep in mind a common mistake: assuming a topic exists when you haven’t verified publishers and subscribers. Use these tools step by step and you’ll often find the cause within minutes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › ROS Tools & Logging
ROS Command-Line Tools and Logging
Use the ROS CLI to inspect nodes, topics, services, parameters and packages. Learn logging levels and where logs are stored so you can debug crashes and runtime errors.
Why this chapter
These tools let you act like a detective: list nodes, inspect connections, replay messages, and read logs so failures become explainable instead of mysterious.
What you’ll do
Run rosnode, rostopic, rosservice, rosparam, rosmsg/rossrv and rospack to inspect systems. Use logging levels and read ~/.ros/log to find errors after crashes.
Explore Key Topics
Node inspection
Use rosnode list/info/ping/kill to see node connections and PID/URI details.
Topic & service tools
rostopic and rosservice let you echo messages, measure rates, and call services for live checks.
Logging & files
Logging levels and ~/.ros/log are essential for post-mortem debugging and dynamic verbosity changes with rqt_logger_level.
Detective toolkit (visual)
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
rosnode
node inspection
rostopic
topic monitoring
logging
levels & files
Starter tip
Begin every debugging session by listing nodes and topics. Verify publishers, subscribers and services before changing code — often the issue is a misnamed topic or mismatched message type.

Second, you will configure ROS logging levels — DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, and FATAL — and learn where those messages appear on the console and in log files. The activities are hands-on: you’ll run commands on turtlesim, inspect connections, and locate logs in your home directory. This screen prepares you to act like a detective when anything in your robot pipeline misbehaves.

screens.title: rosnode — Inspecting nodes and connections
screens.narratorSegment: rosnode is the tool you use to observe the set of nodes running in your ROS environment and learn how they connect. At minimum you will use rosnode list to see every active node and rosnode info with a node name to discover its publications, subscriptions, services, PID and URI. You can also check responsiveness with rosnode ping and remove dead registrations with rosnode cleanup. A common practical workflow is to run rosnode list, then rosnode info for a node that seems misbehaving to confirm whether it publishes the topic you expect. For example, if a controller node should publish to /cmd_vel but does not appear in the node’s publications, the problem may be a startup flag or a mismatched namespace. A typical misconception is assuming a node’s process failed when the registration remains; rosnode cleanup and checking the PID/URI fields will distinguish a stale registration from an actual running process. Practice: launch turtlesim, run rosnode list to find /turtlesim, run rosnode info /turtlesim to see topics and services, then experiment with rosnode ping /some_node and rosnode kill for controlled tests. Takeaway: rosnode tells you who’s present and how they are wired together.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › rosnode
Common rosnode commands
# List all running nodes
rosnode list

# Show detailed information about a node
rosnode info /my_node

# Ping a node
rosnode ping /my_node

# Kill a node
rosnode kill /my_node

# Clean up stale registrations
rosnode cleanup
Example
Inspect turtlesim
Run rosnode list and rosnode info /turtlesim to see its topics and the teleport service. This verifies it is correctly registered.
Common mistake
Assuming registration == running
A node may remain registered after crashing. Check PID/URI or use rosnode ping to confirm it is responsive before killing or restarting.
What rosnode info shows
  • Publications: the topics the node publishes.
  • Subscriptions: topics it listens to.
  • Services: service names it advertises.
  • PID and URI: process and network address for deeper checks.
Key Takeaway
Start every connection debugging session with rosnode list and rosnode info to map the running graph before changing code.

screens.title: rostopic — Inspect topics and message flow
screens.narratorSegment: rostopic is your stethoscope for topic traffic. It helps you list active topics, see what messages look like, measure publishing rate, and even publish test messages. Start with rostopic list to find available topics. When you need details, run rostopic info /topic_name: it shows publishers and subscribers and the message type. To observe live messages, use rostopic echo /topic_name — this prints each arriving message so you can inspect field values. If you suspect timing issues, rostopic hz /topic_name measures the rate, and rostopic bw shows bandwidth usage. You can also publish a test message with rostopic pub to check if subscribers react correctly; for example, rostopic pub /my_topic std_msgs/String "data: 'hello'" will send a single message, while adding -r 10 sends messages at 10Hz. A common trap is mismatched message types: rostopic type /topic_name tells you the exact message struct so you can build the right payload. Practice example: run rostopic echo /turtle1/cmd_vel while driving the turtle to see velocity commands and verify the rate with rostopic hz. Remember to stop verbose echoing when you're done to avoid noisy consoles. Which topic would you echo first when behavior seems wrong?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › rostopic
Useful rostopic commands
# List all active topics
rostopic list

# Show info about a topic
rostopic info /my_topic

# Print messages as they arrive
rostopic echo /my_topic

# Show the message type
rostopic type /my_topic

# Show publishing rate (Hz)
rostopic hz /my_topic

# Show bandwidth
rostopic bw /my_topic

# Publish a message manually
rostopic pub /my_topic std_msgs/String "data: 'hello'"

# Publish repeatedly
rostopic pub -r 10 /my_topic std_msgs/String "data: 'hello'"
Example
Debugging velocity commands
Echo /turtle1/cmd_vel while controlling the turtle. If you see zero velocities when teleop is used, check the publisher and subscriber lists and message types to locate the mismatch.
Pro tip
Use rostopic type before publishing test messages so you format the payload correctly and avoid type errors on the subscriber side.
Key Takeaway
rostopic lets you observe and simulate topic traffic — essential when verifying message flow and timing between nodes.

screens.title: rosservice — Calling and inspecting services
screens.narratorSegment: rosservice is designed to help you inspect and exercise service endpoints. Start with rosservice list to see available services and rosservice info /service_name to learn which node provides that service and its type. To call a service interactively use rosservice call with a request payload that matches the service arguments. For example, calling a teleport service might look like a small YAML-like request with named fields for x, y and theta. Use rosservice type and rosservice args to discover the service message type and argument names before calling. A common misconception is treating services like topics; services are synchronous request/response interactions. If a service call blocks or fails, check which node advertises the service with rosservice info and then inspect that node with rosnode info or logs to see why it rejected requests. Example practice: use rosservice list to find /turtle1/teleport_absolute, run rosservice info to confirm the provider node, then call the service to move the turtle. This workflow helps you verify service availability and correct request formatting. rosservice — Calling and inspecting services means use rosservice info and call to verify that a service is present, provided by the expected node, and accepts your request format.. In practical terms, list services, inspect types and call services for runtime checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › rosservice
Core rosservice commands
# List services
rosservice list

# Show service information
rosservice info /my_service

# Call a service
rosservice call /my_service "request_field: value"

# Show service type
rosservice type /my_service

# Show service args
rosservice args /my_service
Example
teleporting the turtle
Find /turtle1/teleport_absolute with rosservice list, inspect it, then call it with x, y and theta fields to move the turtle instantly.
Service vs Topic
  • Service: synchronous request/response, use rosservice call.
  • Topic: asynchronous publish/subscribe, use rostopic echo and pub.
Key Takeaway
When a service call fails, inspect the provider with rosservice info and the underlying node with rosnode info or logs to find the failure reason.

screens.title: rosparam — Inspecting and managing parameters
screens.narratorSegment: rosparam manages the runtime configuration parameters that many nodes read at startup or during execution. Typical commands are rosparam list to see parameter names, rosparam get to read a value, rosparam set to change a value, rosparam dump to write current parameters to a YAML file, and rosparam load to populate parameters from a YAML file. A practical workflow is to list relevant parameters, get the current value to confirm defaults, then set a temporary value to test behavior without modifying code. For reproducible runs you can dump parameters to params. yaml and later load them before launching your nodes so the same configuration is used. A common mistake is setting parameters only locally in a terminal without saving them; using dump after adjustments ensures you can reuse the configuration. Example: change /background_r for turtlesim with rosparam set /background_r 200, then dump and restart turtlesim to verify persistence. Takeaway: rosparam is your configuration control so you can iterate on settings quickly and reproduce experiments reliably. rosparam — Inspecting and managing parameters means use rosparam get/set/dump/load to test and persist runtime configuration across launches.. In practical terms, list, get, set, dump and load parameters used by nodes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › rosparam
Parameter commands
# List parameters
rosparam list

# Get a parameter value
rosparam get /my_param

# Set a parameter
rosparam set /my_param value

# Dump parameters to a file
rosparam dump params.yaml

# Load parameters from a file
rosparam load params.yaml
Scenario
Tweak turtlesim color
Use rosparam get /background_r, then rosparam set /background_r 200 to change the red component and rosparam dump to save the change for future runs.
Why parameters matter
Parameters let nodes be configured without code edits. They are useful for tuning gains, thresholds, topic names and other runtime options. Always save reproducible configurations with dump/load.
Key Takeaway
Use rosparam to iterate quickly on configuration and persist settings for reproducible launches.

screens.title: rosmsg & rossrv — Read message and service structures
screens.narratorSegment: rosmsg and rossrv let you read the schema of message and service types so you can construct valid messages and requests. Use rosmsg show geometry_msgs/Twist to view fields like linear and angular vectors and their numeric components. For services, rossrv show turtlesim/Spawn displays the required request fields such as x, y and theta. These tools remove guesswork: they show field names, nested message types and the exact structure the publisher or service expects. A common error is publishing with incorrectly named fields or a missing nested structure; rosmsg and rossrv prevent that by making the type explicit. Practice by running rosmsg show std_msgs/String and comparing that to what rostopic echo prints on a topic of that type. Also use rosmsg package std_msgs to list message types available in a package. Takeaway: reading the message or service definition is a short step that prevents many runtime mismatches and type errors. rosmsg & rossrv — Read message and service structures means use rosmsg show and rossrv show to inspect payload fields so publishers and service callers match the expected structure.. In practical terms, inspect fields and nested types to build correct payloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › rosmsg / rossrv
Common commands
# Show message structure
rosmsg show geometry_msgs/Twist

# Show service structure
rossrv show turtlesim/Spawn

# List message types in a package
rosmsg package std_msgs
Example
Verify Twist structure
Use rosmsg show geometry_msgs/Twist to confirm fields like linear.x and angular.z when building or inspecting velocity messages.
Key Takeaway
Always inspect the message or service definition before publishing or calling; it prevents type mismatches that cause silent failures.

screens.title: rospack — Find packages and dependencies
screens.narratorSegment: rospack helps you locate packages on disk and inspect their dependency graph. Use rospack find my_package to get the filesystem path to a package, which is handy when you need to open source files or examine launch files referenced by nodes. rospack depends my_package lists package dependencies so you can check whether missing runtime libraries or messages might cause nodes to fail. rospack list returns all packages known to the current ROS environment. A practical use is when a node reports an import error: find the package directory and inspect setup files, or verify that the right package version is in your workspace. Avoid the mistake of assuming a package is installed globally; rospack find reveals whether your workspace overlay or ROS environment is correctly configured. Example: if a custom node fails to locate a message type, use rospack find to confirm the message package path and then check that the package is sourced in your environment. Takeaway: rospack connects runtime errors to on-disk package structure. rospack — Find packages and dependencies means use rospack to find package locations and dependencies so you can inspect source, launch files, and message definitions when debugging.. In practical terms, locate package paths and list dependencies for troubleshooting builds. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: ROS logging levels and API
screens.narratorSegment: ROS logging uses familiar severity levels you know from other languages: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR and FATAL. DEBUG is for detailed tracing, INFO for general operational messages, WARN for potential problems, ERROR for failures that prevented an operation, and FATAL when the node cannot continue. In Python, use rospy. logdebug, rospy. loginfo, rospy. logwarn, rospy. logerr and rospy. logfatal to emit messages. In C++ the corresponding calls are ROS_DEBUG, ROS_INFO, ROS_WARN, ROS_ERROR and ROS_FATAL. By default INFO level is visible, but DEBUG messages only appear if you increase verbosity. Logs are printed to the console when you set output="screen" in a launch file and are also written to files under ~/. ros/log/. Each launch run creates a timestamped directory containing rosout. log and per-node logs. A common misconception is assuming console output is the only record; always check ~/. ros/log/latest for persistent messages and stack traces after a crash. Example: add rospy. logwarn when the turtle approaches a wall to see warning messages, then open the log files later to search for those warnings. Takeaway: logging levels let you control noise and reveal deeper info during debugging.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › ROS Logging
Severity levels
  • DEBUG — very detailed, only for deep troubleshooting.
  • INFO — normal runtime information (default).
  • WARN — signs of possible problems.
  • ERROR — an operation failed.
  • FATAL — node cannot continue.
API examples
# Python
rospy.logdebug("Debug: x = %f", x)
rospy.loginfo("Node started successfully.")
rospy.logwarn("Battery is low: %d%%", battery)
rospy.logerr("Failed to connect to sensor.")
rospy.logfatal("Critical error: shutting down.")

# C++
ROS_DEBUG("Debug: x = %f", x);
ROS_INFO("Node started successfully.");
ROS_WARN("Battery is low: %d%%", battery);
ROS_ERROR("Failed to connect to sensor.");
ROS_FATAL("Critical error: shutting down.");
Console and files
Set output="screen" in launch to stream logs to the console. All messages are also written to ~/.ros/log/ in a new timestamped directory per run, including rosout.log and per-node logs.
Key Takeaway
Control verbosity with levels and always check ~/.ros/log/latest when investigating crashes or errors.

screens.title: Setting logging levels and rqt_logger_level
screens.narratorSegment: There are two reliable ways to change logging verbosity. First, set environment or node logger level in a launch file so the node starts with the desired verbosity. For example, set ROS_PYTHON_LOG_LEVEL to DEBUG for a Python node in a launch entry. Second, use rqt_logger_level — a GUI tool — to adjust logging levels of running nodes without restarting them. This is very useful when you want additional detail for a short time and then reduce noise. A practical pattern is to set INFO by default, switch a misbehaving node to DEBUG with rqt_logger_level while reproducing the issue, then examine ~/. ros/log/latest for the new messages. You can also programmatically set logger levels via the roscpp or rospy APIs for finer control. Beware over-logging: leaving DEBUG on will flood logs and can make it harder to find important ERROR entries. Example: reproduce a problem while emitting DEBUG traces, then set the node back to INFO to restore normal logging. The takeaway is to use dynamic level changes to collect targeted evidence without long-term log noise. Setting logging levels and rqt_logger_level means use launch-time settings for planned debugging and rqt_logger_level for on-demand, non-restart increases in verbosity.. In practical terms, change verbosity in launch files and dynamically at runtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Log files and roslaunch output options
screens.narratorSegment: ROS writes runtime logs to a directory under your home directory so you can inspect messages after a node crashes or the system is shut down. Each roslaunch run creates a timestamped directory under ~/. ros/log/ that contains rosout. log — an aggregated log stream — and per-node log files like my_node-1. log. If you set output="screen" for a node in a launch file, that node’s messages also appear on your console while it runs, which is convenient for live debugging. After a crash, open ~/. ros/log/latest/ or the timestamped directory to find error messages and stack traces. One workflow is to reproduce the failure while streaming logs to the console with output="screen" then immediately check rosout. log for the full trace. A common misconception is expecting transient console output to persist; always inspect the log files because they capture the complete history. Example: after making a node print a WARN when the turtle hits a wall, find that WARN line in ~/. ros/log/latest/rosout. log to confirm the event time and context. Takeaway: combine console output with the persistent logs in ~/. ros/log/ to perform effective post-mortem debugging.

Where logs are stored

screens.title: Diagnostic checklist: node publishes but subscriber receives nothing
screens.narratorSegment: When a publisher appears to send messages but a subscriber receives nothing follow a short diagnostic checklist. First, run rostopic list to confirm the topic exists. Second, run rostopic info /topic_name to confirm both the publisher and subscriber are registered and that the message type matches. Third, use rosnode info /publisher_node to ensure the publisher is publishing the expected topic and inspect the node’s publications. Fourth, run rostopic echo /topic_name to confirm messages actually appear on the wire; if not, the publisher may not be producing messages even though it registered. Fifth, run rosnode info /subscriber_node to confirm it subscribes to the correct topic and not a misspelled variant. If the type is mismatched, rosmsg show the message type to discover correct field names and structure. Finally, check ~/. ros/log/latest/ for any ERROR lines or tracebacks from the subscriber or publisher that explain a crash or rejected messages. A common misconception is to restart nodes before checking connections; the sequence above saves time by identifying misconfiguration, naming errors, or type mismatches before restarting. By following these steps you can usually find the issue without changing code.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn to use ROS’s command-line toolkit and logging system so you can inspect running nodes, monitor topic traffic, call services, manage parameters, and find the log files that explain failures. These commands are your primary debugging tools — they let you explore the system without editing code and they help you isolate where messages, services, or configuration are going wrong. We’ll show concrete terminal examples so you can practice listing nodes, echoing topic messages, calling services, and changing logging levels. You will also learn where ROS stores log files and how the logging severity levels map to practical debugging choices. By the end you should be able to follow a simple diagnostic checklist when a node stops responding and find the log entry or service error that explains the failure. Keep in mind a common mistake: assuming a topic exists when you haven’t verified publishers and subscribers. Use these tools step by step and you’ll often find the cause within minutes.

In this first objectives screen we set measurable goals so you can check your progress. You will learn to use rosnode, rostopic, rosservice, rosparam, rosmsg, rossrv, and rospack to inspect a running ROS system. Practically, that means listing nodes and topics, querying message types, echoing live messages, calling services, and locating package paths. Second, you will configure ROS logging levels — DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, and FATAL — and learn where those messages appear on the console and in log files. Understanding how logging maps to behavior helps you decide when to increase verbosity for troubleshooting. Each objective includes a concrete example and a small mnemonic so you can recall which tool to reach for. The activities are hands-on: you’ll run commands on turtlesim, inspect connections, and locate logs in your home directory. This screen prepares you to act like a detective when anything in your robot pipeline misbehaves.

This second objectives screen focuses on measurable demonstrations. For inspection skills you will run rosnode list and rostopic list to enumerate runtime entities and then use rosnode info and rostopic info to verify publishers, subscribers, and service providers. For parameter skills you will get and set values with rosparam get and rosparam set and show how to dump and load parameters to and from YAML files. For message literacy you will use rosmsg show and rossrv show to read field names and nested types so you can form correct messages or service requests. For logging competency you will change the log level using environment settings in a launch file and by using rqt_logger_level during runtime, then open ~/. ros/log/latest/rosout. log to locate errors and stack traces. Each objective includes a short mnemonic so you remember which command to try first during a real debugging session.

rosnode is the tool you use to observe the set of nodes running in your ROS environment and learn how they connect. At minimum you will use rosnode list to see every active node and rosnode info with a node name to discover its publications, subscriptions, services, PID and URI. You can also check responsiveness with rosnode ping and remove dead registrations with rosnode cleanup. A common practical workflow is to run rosnode list, then rosnode info for a node that seems misbehaving to confirm whether it publishes the topic you expect. For example, if a controller node should publish to /cmd_vel but does not appear in the node’s publications, the problem may be a startup flag or a mismatched namespace. A typical misconception is assuming a node’s process failed when the registration remains; rosnode cleanup and checking the PID/URI fields will distinguish a stale registration from an actual running process. Practice: launch turtlesim, run rosnode list to find /turtlesim, run rosnode info /turtlesim to see topics and services, then experiment with rosnode ping /some_node and rosnode kill for controlled tests. Takeaway: rosnode tells you who’s present and how they are wired together.

rostopic is your stethoscope for topic traffic. It helps you list active topics, see what messages look like, measure publishing rate, and even publish test messages. Start with rostopic list to find available topics. When you need details, run rostopic info /topic_name: it shows publishers and subscribers and the message type. To observe live messages, use rostopic echo /topic_name — this prints each arriving message so you can inspect field values. If you suspect timing issues, rostopic hz /topic_name measures the rate, and rostopic bw shows bandwidth usage. You can also publish a test message with rostopic pub to check if subscribers react correctly; for example, rostopic pub /my_topic std_msgs/String "data: 'hello'" will send a single message, while adding -r 10 sends messages at 10Hz. A common trap is mismatched message types: rostopic type /topic_name tells you the exact message struct so you can build the right payload. Practice example: run rostopic echo /turtle1/cmd_vel while driving the turtle to see velocity commands and verify the rate with rostopic hz. Remember to stop verbose echoing when you're done to avoid noisy consoles. Which topic would you echo first when behavior seems wrong?

rosservice is designed to help you inspect and exercise service endpoints. Start with rosservice list to see available services and rosservice info /service_name to learn which node provides that service and its type. To call a service interactively use rosservice call with a request payload that matches the service arguments. For example, calling a teleport service might look like a small YAML-like request with named fields for x, y and theta. Use rosservice type and rosservice args to discover the service message type and argument names before calling. A common misconception is treating services like topics; services are synchronous request/response interactions. If a service call blocks or fails, check which node advertises the service with rosservice info and then inspect that node with rosnode info or logs to see why it rejected requests. Example practice: use rosservice list to find /turtle1/teleport_absolute, run rosservice info to confirm the provider node, then call the service to move the turtle. This workflow helps you verify service availability and correct request formatting. rosservice — Calling and inspecting services means use rosservice info and call to verify that a service is present, provided by the expected node, and accepts your request format.. In practical terms, list services, inspect types and call services for runtime checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

rosparam manages the runtime configuration parameters that many nodes read at startup or during execution. Typical commands are rosparam list to see parameter names, rosparam get to read a value, rosparam set to change a value, rosparam dump to write current parameters to a YAML file, and rosparam load to populate parameters from a YAML file. A practical workflow is to list relevant parameters, get the current value to confirm defaults, then set a temporary value to test behavior without modifying code. For reproducible runs you can dump parameters to params. yaml and later load them before launching your nodes so the same configuration is used. A common mistake is setting parameters only locally in a terminal without saving them; using dump after adjustments ensures you can reuse the configuration. Example: change /background_r for turtlesim with rosparam set /background_r 200, then dump and restart turtlesim to verify persistence. Takeaway: rosparam is your configuration control so you can iterate on settings quickly and reproduce experiments reliably. rosparam — Inspecting and managing parameters means use rosparam get/set/dump/load to test and persist runtime configuration across launches.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

These tools remove guesswork: they show field names, nested message types and the exact structure the publisher or service expects. A common error is publishing with incorrectly named fields or a missing nested structure; rosmsg and rossrv prevent that by making the type explicit. Practice by running rosmsg show std_msgs/String and comparing that to what rostopic echo prints on a topic of that type. Also use rosmsg package std_msgs to list message types available in a package. Takeaway: logging levels let you control noise and reveal deeper info during debugging.

There are two reliable ways to change logging verbosity. First, set environment or node logger level in a launch file so the node starts with the desired verbosity. For example, set ROS_PYTHON_LOG_LEVEL to DEBUG for a Python node in a launch entry. Second, use rqt_logger_level — a GUI tool — to adjust logging levels of running nodes without restarting them. This is very useful when you want additional detail for a short time and then reduce noise. A practical pattern is to set INFO by default, switch a misbehaving node to DEBUG with rqt_logger_level while reproducing the issue, then examine ~/. ros/log/latest for the new messages. You can also programmatically set logger levels via the roscpp or rospy APIs for finer control. Beware over-logging: leaving DEBUG on will flood logs and can make it harder to find important ERROR entries. Example: reproduce a problem while emitting DEBUG traces, then set the node back to INFO to restore normal logging. The takeaway is to use dynamic level changes to collect targeted evidence without long-term log noise. Setting logging levels and rqt_logger_level means use launch-time settings for planned debugging and rqt_logger_level for on-demand, non-restart increases in verbosity.. ROS writes runtime logs to a directory under your home directory so you can inspect messages after a node crashes or the system is shut down. Each roslaunch run creates a timestamped directory under ~/. ros/log/ that contains rosout. log — an aggregated log stream — and per-node log files like my_node-1. log. If you set output="screen" for a node in a launch file, that node’s messages also appear on your console while it runs, which is convenient for live debugging. After a crash, open ~/. ros/log/latest/ or the timestamped directory to find error messages and stack traces. One workflow is to reproduce the failure while streaming logs to the console with output="screen" then immediately check rosout. log for the full trace. A common misconception is expecting transient console output to persist; always inspect the log files because they capture the complete history. Example: after making a node print a WARN when the turtle hits a wall, find that WARN line in ~/. ros/log/latest/rosout. log to confirm the event time and context. Takeaway: combine console output with the persistent logs in ~/. ros/log/ to perform effective post-mortem debugging.

When a publisher appears to send messages but a subscriber receives nothing follow a short diagnostic checklist. First, run rostopic list to confirm the topic exists. Second, run rostopic info /topic_name to confirm both the publisher and subscriber are registered and that the message type matches. Third, use rosnode info /publisher_node to ensure the publisher is publishing the expected topic and inspect the node’s publications. Fourth, run rostopic echo /topic_name to confirm messages actually appear on the wire; if not, the publisher may not be producing messages even though it registered. Fifth, run rosnode info /subscriber_node to confirm it subscribes to the correct topic and not a misspelled variant. If the type is mismatched, rosmsg show the message type to discover correct field names and structure. Finally, check ~/. ros/log/latest/ for any ERROR lines or tracebacks from the subscriber or publisher that explain a crash or rejected messages. A common misconception is to restart nodes before checking connections; the sequence above saves time by identifying misconfiguration, naming errors, or type mismatches before restarting. By following these steps you can usually find the issue without changing code.

Let’s summarize the essential tools and ideas you should retain. rosnode tells you which processes are registered and how they connect. rostopic lets you observe and simulate topic traffic and measure rates. rosservice allows you to inspect and call synchronous services. rosparam manages runtime configuration that nodes consume. rosmsg and rossrv reveal message and service field structures so you can form valid payloads. rospack maps runtime problems to package files on disk. Finally, ROS logging with levels DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR and FATAL records evidence both to the console (when configured) and to persistent log directories under ~/. ros/log/. Mastering these tools gives you a systematic approach to debugging: verify existence, inspect connections and types, reproduce the issue, increase verbosity if needed, then examine persistent logs. Keep three quick reminders in mind as you debug ROS systems. First, inspect before changing: list nodes and topics and verify connections and types before touching code. Second, use targeted verbosity: enable DEBUG only for focused investigation and revert to INFO afterwards to avoid noisy logs. Third, persist and review evidence: use rosparam dump and ~/. ros/log/latest to save configuration and examine full traces after crashes. These short rules help you stay efficient, avoid chasing symptoms, and gather the facts you need to fix the root cause.
